topics.title: Why classify data? Raw data and classification

learn.hook: A kabadiwala's cart is a jumble of newspapers, bottles, tins and plastic. Within minutes he sorts it into neat heaps, because sorted scrap is easy to price and sell. Data work the same way.
points: Raw (unclassified) data are data in the form they were collected: large, disorganised and hard to handle. Even finding the highest value or the average is tedious.
Classification arranges data into groups or classes according to some common feature, so the data become easy to understand, compare and analyse.
Each classification must follow a clear criterion (basis), e.g. by year, by state, by gender or by income range.
Advantages: brings order, highlights similarities and differences, makes comparison possible, and prepares data for tabulation and analysis.

example.q: Marks of 20 students are recorded in roll-number order: 47, 85, 32, 61, 75, 52, 90, 38, 64, 71, 29, 55, 83, 49, 66, 78, 41, 58, 69, 93. How many scored 60 or more? Why is this slow?
steps: Count: 11 students scored 60 or more.
We had to check every value because the data are raw and unordered.
example.answer: 11 students; raw data force us to inspect every value, which classification avoids.

learn.reallife: The RBI classifies bank loans by sector (agriculture, industry, services, personal loans) so it can quickly see where credit is flowing.

Classified data make comparison easier.
Similar items grouped together are easy to compare.
Finding the highest value in raw data is always quick.
With large raw data you must scan every value.
A kabadiwala sorting scrap is an analogy for classification.

quiz.q: Data in their original, unorganised form are called:
quiz.explain: Unprocessed data as collected are raw data.
steps: Asked: the name for data in their original, unorganised form.
Rule: data exactly as collected, before any processing, are raw data.
Classified, tabulated and grouped data have already been organised.
So the answer is 'Raw data'.
Answer: Raw data
quiz.mistake: Thinks 'raw' refers to wrong data

quiz.q: The main purpose of classification is to:
options: Bring order to data so they can be analysed
quiz.explain: Classification organises data into groups for easy understanding and analysis.
steps: Asked: the main purpose of classification.
Classification arranges data into groups of similar items.
This brings order so data can be understood and analysed.
It does not enlarge data, hide values or replace collection → 'Bring order to data so they can be analysed'.
Answer: Bring order to data so they can be analysed
quiz.mistake: Thinks classification changes or removes data

quiz.q: Which is a valid criterion for classifying a list of workers?
quiz.explain: A classification needs a clear, relevant basis such as wage level.
steps: Asked: a valid basis for classifying workers.
Rule: a classification needs a clear, relevant basis.
Monthly wages are a measurable feature of each worker.
Guesses, the interviewer's mood or questionnaire order are not features of workers → 'Their monthly wages'.
Answer: Their monthly wages
quiz.mistake: Accepts an arbitrary basis for grouping

quiz.q: From the raw marks 34, 67, 89, 45, 72, 56, 91, 38, how many are below 50?
quiz.explain: Below 50: 34, 45, 38, so 3 values.
steps: Check each value against 50
34, 45, 38 are below 50
Count = 3
Answer: 3
quiz.mistake: Counts 50 itself or misses a value

quiz.q: From the same raw marks (34, 67, 89, 45, 72, 56, 91, 38), what is the difference between the highest and lowest value?
quiz.explain: Highest = 91, lowest = 34, difference = 57. With raw data you must scan every value to find them.
steps: Highest = 91
Lowest = 34
Answer: 57
quiz.mistake: Picks the wrong extreme values

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Classified data are more useful than raw data for analysis.
Reason (R): Classification groups similar items, making comparison and analysis easier.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Grouping makes patterns visible, which is why classified data aid analysis.
steps: A: classified data are more useful than raw data for analysis → true.
R: classification groups similar items, easing comparison → true.
Grouping makes patterns visible, which is why classified data help analysis.
So R explains A → both true and R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Sees no benefit in classification

quiz.q: Why is it tedious to find the average from a large mass of raw data?
options: Because raw data have no numbers
Because the values are scattered without order and every value must be handled separately
Because raw data are always wrong
quiz.explain: Without grouping, every individual value must be processed.
steps: Asked: why finding an average from a large mass of raw data is tedious.
Raw data are scattered with no order.
Each value must be handled separately.
Raw data do have numbers and are not always wrong → 'Because the values are scattered without order and every value must be handled separately'.
Answer: Because the values are scattered without order and every value must be handled separately
quiz.mistake: Thinks raw data cannot be used at all

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT an advantage of classification?
options: It guarantees that data are free of errors
quiz.explain: Classification organises data; it cannot correct errors made during collection.
steps: Asked: which is NOT an advantage of classification.
Classification brings order, eases comparison and prepares data for tabulation.
It only organises data; it cannot fix errors made during collection.
So 'It guarantees that data are free of errors' is not an advantage.
Answer: It guarantees that data are free of errors
quiz.mistake: Thinks organising data also makes them accurate

teach.ask: Gappu has a heap of 500 bird weights scribbled randomly. 'It's a mess! Why and how should I classify it?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Raw data are messy; grouping by a clear basis makes them easy to compare and analyse!
teach.nudge: Good start! On what basis would you group the weights? And what does grouping help me do?

revise.summary: Raw data are data in the form collected: large, disorganised and hard to handle. Classification arranges data into groups by a clear common feature so they are easy to understand, compare and analyse.

traps: 'Raw' does not mean wrong data: it means data as collected
Classification organises data; it does not make them error-free

learn.hook: India's GDP by year, rainfall by state, workers by gender, and students by marks are four different ways to slice data. Each answers a different question.
points: Chronological (temporal): by time, such as years or months. Such data form a time series (e.g. India's population 1951–2011).
Spatial (geographical): by place, such as country, state, district (e.g. wheat output by state).
Qualitative: by attributes that cannot be measured, such as gender, marital status, religion. Classifying by several attributes at once (e.g. sex, then married/unmarried) is manifold classification.
Quantitative: by measurable characteristics such as marks, height, income, grouped into classes like 0–10, 10–20.
Relative frequency of a class = class frequency ÷ total frequency; it can be shown as a percentage (× 100).

example.q: In a class of 50, the 30–40 marks class has 15 students. Find its relative frequency and percentage.
steps: Relative frequency = 15 / 50 = 0.3
Percentage = 0.3 × 100 = 30%

learn.reallife: The Economic Survey shows exports by year (chronological), by destination country (spatial) and by commodity group (qualitative), all from the same trade data.

quiz.q: Classification of data according to time is called:
quiz.explain: Classifying by years, months or days is chronological (temporal).
steps: Asked: the name for classification by time.
Rule: grouping by years, months or days is chronological (temporal) classification.
Spatial is by place; qualitative is by attribute; quantitative is by measured value.
So the answer is 'Chronological classification'.
Answer: Chronological classification
quiz.mistake: Mixes up chronological with spatial

quiz.q: Data on cotton production in Gujarat, Maharashtra and Telangana are an example of:
quiz.explain: Classifying by place (states) is spatial or geographical.
steps: Asked: the type of classification for cotton output by state.
Gujarat, Maharashtra and Telangana are places.
Rule: classification by place is spatial (geographical).
So the answer is 'Spatial classification'.
Answer: Spatial classification
quiz.mistake: Thinks any data with names is qualitative

quiz.q: Classifying a population first by sex, then each group by literate/illiterate, is called:
quiz.explain: Classification by more than one attribute is manifold classification.
steps: Asked: the name for classifying first by sex, then by literacy.
Two attributes are used one after another.
Rule: classification by more than one attribute is manifold classification.
Simple classification uses only one attribute → 'Manifold classification'.
Answer: Manifold classification
quiz.mistake: Does not know the term for multi-attribute classification

quiz.q: Grouping workers by their daily wages into ₹200–300, ₹300–400 and so on is:
quiz.explain: Wages are measurable, so this is quantitative classification.
steps: Asked: the type when workers are grouped by daily wage ranges.
Daily wage is measured in rupees, a number.
Rule: grouping by a measurable characteristic is quantitative classification.
So the answer is 'Quantitative classification'.
Answer: Quantitative classification
quiz.mistake: Confuses measurable characteristics with attributes

quiz.q: Out of 80 households, 20 fall in the income class ₹20,000–30,000. What is the relative frequency of this class?
steps: Relative frequency = class frequency / total
Answer: 0.25
quiz.mistake: Divides the total by the class frequency (80/20 = 4)

quiz.q: In a survey of 200 people, 46 are in the 20–30 years age class. What percentage of people does this class hold?
steps: Percentage = 46/200 × 100
Answer: 23%
quiz.mistake: Treats the class frequency itself as a percentage

quiz.q: A time series is produced by which type of classification?
quiz.explain: Arranging values by time gives a time series.
steps: Asked: the classification that produces a time series.
A time series lists values arranged by time.
Rule: arranging data by time is chronological classification.
So the answer is 'Chronological'.
Answer: Chronological
quiz.mistake: Thinks a time series is arranged by place

quiz.q: The relative frequencies of all classes in a distribution add up to:
quiz.explain: Each is class frequency ÷ total, so together they sum to total ÷ total = 1 (or 100%).
steps: Rule: relative frequency of a class = class frequency ÷ total frequency.
Adding all classes: (f₁ + f₂ + … + fₙ) ÷ total.
The numerator equals the total, so the sum = total ÷ total.
Sum of relative frequencies = 1 (or 100%).
Answer: 1
quiz.mistake: Confuses proportions with percentages or counts

teach.ask: Gappu has data on bird counts by year, by forest, by colour and by weight. 'Are these different kinds of classification? Teach me!'
teach.praise: Tweet! By time, by place, by attribute, and by measurable value: four kinds of classification!
teach.nudge: Good! You listed some kinds. What do we call classification by place, or by a feature like colour?

revise.summary: Data can be classified chronologically (by time), spatially (by place), qualitatively (by attributes) or quantitatively (by measurable classes). Relative frequency of a class is its frequency divided by the total frequency.
focus: Identify the four kinds of classification from examples
Know manifold classification and that chronological data form a time series
Calculate relative frequency and its percentage
remember: Relative frequency = class frequency ÷ total frequency (× 100 for a percentage)
Manifold classification: classifying by several attributes at once
Relative frequencies of all classes add up to 1 (or 100%)
traps: Don't mix up chronological (time) with spatial (place) classification
Don't divide the total by the class frequency: divide class frequency by the total
Measurable characteristics like wages give quantitative, not qualitative, classification

learn.hook: Your height can be 162.37 cm, but the number of siblings you have can never be 2.5. That difference decides how data are grouped.
points: A variable is a characteristic whose value changes from unit to unit and can be measured, e.g. income, height, marks. An attribute (like gender) is qualitative and is not measured in numbers.
A continuous variable can take any value within a range, including fractions and decimals: height, weight, time, temperature, rainfall, area, age.
A discrete variable takes only certain values (usually whole numbers) and changes in jumps: number of students, cars, children, the number on a dice.
Tip: if you measure it, it is usually continuous; if you count it, it is usually discrete.

example.q: Classify: (a) area of a farm, (b) number on a rolled dice, (c) population of a city, (d) rainfall in a month, (e) age.
steps: Area can be 2.35 hectares: continuous.
Dice shows only 1–6: discrete.
Population is a count of people: discrete.
Rainfall can be 112.6 mm: continuous.
Age can be 15 years 4 months: continuous.
example.answer: Continuous: area, rainfall, age. Discrete: dice number, population.

learn.reallife: IMD reports rainfall to the nearest millimetre (a continuous variable), while Indian Railways counts passengers (a discrete variable).

games.title: Variable facts
items: Age is a discrete variable.
Age can take any fractional value, so it is continuous.
The number shown on a dice is discrete.
It can only be 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 or 6.
Marital status is a variable measured in numbers.
It is an attribute (qualitative).
Rainfall can take fractional values, so it is continuous.
112.6 mm is a valid value.
A discrete variable changes in jumps.
There are gaps between its possible values.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a continuous variable?
options: Number of students in a class
Number of books on a shelf
quiz.explain: Weight can take any value in a range, such as 2.85 kg.
steps: Asked: which is a continuous variable.
Rule: a continuous variable can take any value in a range, including fractions.
Students, goals and books are counted in whole numbers.
Weight can be 2.85 kg → 'Weight of a newborn baby'.
Answer: Weight of a newborn baby
quiz.mistake: Thinks any variable measured in whole numbers in practice is discrete

quiz.q: Which of these is a discrete variable?
options: Number of tractors in a village
quiz.explain: Tractors are counted in whole numbers.
steps: Asked: which is a discrete variable.
Rule: a discrete variable takes only separate values, usually whole numbers.
Temperature, rainfall and height can take fractional values.
Tractors are counted 1, 2, 3 … → 'Number of tractors in a village'.
Answer: Number of tractors in a village
quiz.mistake: Confuses counting with measuring

quiz.q: A variable that can take any value, including fractions, within a range is called:
quiz.explain: That is the definition of a continuous variable.
steps: Asked: the name for a variable that can take any value, including fractions, in a range.
Rule: this is the definition of a continuous variable.
A discrete variable takes only separate values; attributes are qualities.
So the answer is 'Continuous'.
Answer: Continuous
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the two types

quiz.q: The number obtained on rolling a dice is:
quiz.explain: It can only be one of six whole numbers.
steps: Asked: the type of variable 'number on a rolled dice'.
The result can only be 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 or 6.
No value in between (like 2.5) is possible.
So it is a discrete variable.
Answer: A discrete variable
quiz.mistake: Thinks anything random is continuous

quiz.q: How many possible values can the variable 'number on a standard dice' take?
quiz.explain: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6: six values, which is why it is discrete.
steps: Possible faces of a standard dice: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6.
Count them: 6 values.
No fractions are possible, so the list is complete.
Number of possible values = 6.
Answer: 6
quiz.mistake: Thinks a discrete variable can take infinitely many values in a small range

quiz.q: Which pair has one continuous and one discrete variable?
options: Number of cars and number of buses
Time taken and number of students
quiz.explain: Time is continuous; number of students is discrete.
steps: Asked: the pair with one continuous and one discrete variable.
Time taken can be any value such as 4.5 minutes → continuous.
Number of students is counted in whole numbers → discrete.
Height & weight and rainfall & temperature are both continuous; cars & buses are both discrete.
Answer: Time taken and number of students
quiz.mistake: Does not check each variable separately

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Population of a city is a discrete variable.
Reason (R): Population can take any fractional value.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Population is a count of people, so it takes only whole numbers; R is false.
steps: A: population of a city is discrete → true, it is a count of people.
R: population can take any fractional value → false, there is no half a person.
So the reason given is wrong.
A is true but R is false.
Answer: A is true but R is false
quiz.mistake: Thinks large numbers make a variable continuous

quiz.q: What is the main difference between a variable and an attribute?
options: A variable can be measured numerically; an attribute is a quality that cannot be directly measured
quiz.explain: Variables (income, height) are quantitative; attributes (gender, honesty) are qualitative.
steps: Asked: the difference between a variable and an attribute.
A variable (income, height) can be measured in numbers.
An attribute (gender, honesty) is a quality that cannot be directly measured.
So 'A variable can be measured numerically; an attribute is a quality that cannot be directly measured' is correct; 'no difference' is wrong.
Answer: A variable can be measured numerically; an attribute is a quality that cannot be directly measured
quiz.mistake: Treats attributes and variables as the same thing

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'My feather length and my number of eggs: are they the same kind of variable? Teach me!'
teach.praise: Tweet! Feather length can be any value: continuous. Eggs are counted in whole numbers: discrete!
teach.nudge: Good! But can I lay 2.5 eggs? Which kind of variable takes only whole-number values?

revise.summary: A continuous variable can take any value in a range, including fractions; a discrete variable takes only certain values, usually whole numbers. A variable is measured in numbers, while an attribute is a quality.
focus: Classify variables as continuous or discrete
Tell a variable from an attribute
Use the tip: measured → usually continuous; counted → usually discrete
remember: Continuous: height, weight, time, temperature, rainfall, area, age
Discrete: number of students, cars, children, the number on a dice
traps: Large numbers do not make a variable continuous: population is discrete
Don't treat a variable as discrete just because it is recorded in whole numbers in practice (e.g. weight)
Don't treat attributes and variables as the same thing

learn.hook: The marks of 1,000 board candidates fit on one small table once you group them into classes like 40–50 and 50–60. That table is a frequency distribution.
points: A frequency distribution shows how the values of a variable are spread across classes, with the number of values (frequency) in each class.
Class: a group of values such as 20–30. Class limits: the lowest (lower limit) and highest (upper limit) values of a class. Class frequency: the number of observations in the class.
Class interval (class width) = upper class limit − lower class limit, e.g. 30 − 20 = 10.
Class mark (mid-point) = (upper limit + lower limit) / 2. It represents the whole class in calculations.
Range = largest value − smallest value. A frequency curve is drawn by plotting frequencies against class marks and joining the points smoothly.

example.q: For the class 40–60: find the class width and class mark. If the data range from 12 to 97, find the range.
steps: Class width = 60 − 40 = 20
Class mark = (40 + 60)/2 = 50

learn.reallife: Pay commissions publish salary bands like ₹25,000–35,000; HR teams use the band's mid-point to estimate average pay.

games.title: Match the term to its meaning
pairs: Number of observations in a class
Smallest value a class can hold

items.q: Range if max is 88 and min is 23

quiz.q: The class mark of the class 30–50 is:
steps: Class mark = (lower + upper)/2
Answer: 40
quiz.mistake: Subtracts the limits (gives width 20) instead of averaging

quiz.q: The class interval (width) of the class 15–25 is:
steps: Rule: class interval (width) = upper limit − lower limit.
Given class 15–25: upper limit = 25, lower limit = 15.
So the class interval is 10.
Answer: 10
quiz.mistake: Adds the limits or gives the mid-point

quiz.q: The lowest value in a data set is 18 and the highest is 96. What is the range?
steps: Range = largest − smallest
Answer: 78
quiz.mistake: Adds the extremes instead of subtracting

quiz.q: The mid-point of a class is 45 and its lower limit is 40. What is the upper limit?
steps: Answer: 50
quiz.mistake: Adds the mid-point and lower limit directly

quiz.q: The class mark of a class is used in calculations because:
options: It is the largest value in the class
It represents all the values in that class
quiz.explain: Once data are grouped, each value in a class is represented by the mid-point.
steps: Asked: why the class mark is used in calculations.
After grouping, the separate values inside a class are no longer listed.
The mid-point (class mark) stands for all values in that class.
It is not the largest value and does not remove errors → 'It represents all the values in that class'.
Answer: It represents all the values in that class
quiz.mistake: Thinks the class mark is a frequency

quiz.q: A frequency curve is obtained by plotting:
options: Frequencies against class marks and joining them by a smooth curve
quiz.explain: Frequencies are plotted against class marks and joined smoothly.
steps: Asked: how a frequency curve is drawn.
Plot each class frequency against its class mark.
Join the points with a smooth freehand curve.
Cumulative frequency is used for an ogive, not a frequency curve → 'Frequencies against class marks and joining them by a smooth curve'.
Answer: Frequencies against class marks and joining them by a smooth curve
quiz.mistake: Confuses the frequency curve with an ogive

quiz.q: The class marks of consecutive equal classes are 25, 35, 45. What is the class width?
quiz.explain: With equal classes, the gap between consecutive class marks equals the class width: 35 − 25 = 10.
steps: Width = difference of consecutive mid-points
Answer: 10
quiz.mistake: Takes the first class mark as the width

quiz.q: Consecutive class marks are 25, 35, 45 and the class width is 10. What are the limits of the first class?
steps: Half width = 5
Answer: 20–30
quiz.mistake: Uses the class mark as the lower limit

teach.ask: Gappu sees '20–30: 12 birds' and asks: 'What are the class limits, the class mark and the frequency here?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Limits 20 and 30, width 10, class mark 25, frequency 12. I can read a frequency table now!
teach.nudge: Good! Can you also tell me the middle value of the class, and how wide it is?

revise.summary: A frequency distribution shows how values of a variable spread across classes, with the frequency of each class. Key terms are class limits, class interval, class mark, class frequency and range.
focus: Calculate class interval, class mark and range
Find a missing class limit from the class mark
Find class width and limits from consecutive class marks
Know how a frequency curve is drawn
remember: Class interval = upper class limit − lower class limit
traps: Don't subtract the limits to get the class mark: average them
Don't add the extremes for the range: subtract
A frequency curve plots frequencies against class marks; don't confuse it with an ogive

learn.hook: Too few classes and you lose the shape of the data; too many and the table is as messy as the raw data. The art is choosing the right classes.
points: Decide equal or unequal classes: equal classes are usual; unequal classes suit data with a very wide range or values bunched in one area (e.g. incomes).
Number of classes is usually between 6 and 15. Number of classes = range ÷ class width (round up to a whole number).
Class limits should be clear and avoid gaps or overlaps. Open-ended classes (like 'below 10' or '90 and above') are avoided where possible because they have no mid-point.
Tally marks count frequencies in groups of five: four strokes and a fifth crossing them (𝍸).
Grouping causes loss of information: once grouped, every value in a class is treated as if it were equal to the class mark.

example.q: Marks range from 30 to 99. You want exclusive classes of width 10. How many classes are needed, and what are they?
steps: Number of classes = 69 / 10 = 6.9, round up to 7

learn.reallife: Income tax slabs are a frequency-style grouping with unequal classes, because incomes are spread over a very wide range.

games.title: Building classes
items: The number of classes is usually between 6 and 15.
This keeps the table readable without losing too much detail.
Open-ended classes are preferred because they have clear mid-points.
Open-ended classes have no defined mid-point, so they are avoided.
Grouping data causes some loss of information.
Individual values are replaced by the class mark.
Unequal classes may suit income data with a very wide range.
They avoid many near-empty classes.
A tally mark group shows ten observations.
Each tally group shows five observations.

quiz.q: Data range from 10 to 89. With a class width of 10, how many classes are needed?
quiz.explain: Range = 89 − 10 = 79, and 79/10 = 7.9, which is rounded up to 8 classes (10–20 up to 80–90).
steps: Round up: 8 classes
Answer: 8
quiz.mistake: Rounds 7.9 down, or forgets to divide the range by the width

quiz.q: Which situation calls for unequal class intervals?
options: Marks of a class test out of 50
Heights of students between 140 and 180 cm
Incomes ranging from ₹5,000 to ₹50 lakh with most below ₹50,000
quiz.explain: A huge range with bunching at one end is better shown with unequal classes.
steps: Asked: when unequal class intervals are needed.
Unequal classes suit data with a huge range and bunching at one end.
Incomes from ₹5,000 to ₹50 lakh with most below ₹50,000 fit this.
Test marks, heights and ages have small ranges → the income option.
Answer: Incomes ranging from ₹5,000 to ₹50 lakh with most below ₹50,000
quiz.mistake: Thinks equal classes always work

quiz.q: Open-ended classes such as 'Above 80' are generally avoided because:
options: They make the table too long
quiz.explain: Without an upper limit, the class mark cannot be found, which hampers calculations.
steps: Asked: why open-ended classes like 'Above 80' are avoided.
Class mark = (lower + upper)/2 needs both limits.
'Above 80' has no upper limit, so its mid-point cannot be found.
That hampers calculations → 'They have no defined mid-point'.
Answer: They have no defined mid-point
quiz.mistake: Does not see the problem with missing limits

quiz.q: In tally marking, the fifth observation is shown by:
options: A stroke crossing the previous four
quiz.explain: The fifth stroke crosses the first four, making a bundle of five.
steps: Asked: how the fifth tally mark is drawn.
Four observations are shown as four vertical strokes.
The fifth is a stroke drawn across the first four.
This makes a bundle of five that is easy to count.
Answer: A stroke crossing the previous four
quiz.mistake: Does not know the convention for groups of five

quiz.q: If 4 complete tally groups and 3 extra strokes are marked against a class, its frequency is:
steps: Each bundle = 5
Answer: 23
quiz.mistake: Counts each tally group as one or adds 4 and 3

quiz.q: The values 21, 22, 23 and 28 fall in the class 20–30. After grouping, what single value represents each of them?
quiz.explain: Every value in the class is represented by the class mark (20 + 30)/2 = 25. This is the loss of information in grouping.
steps: After grouping, each value in a class is represented by its class mark.
Class mark = (lower limit + upper limit)/2.
So 21, 22, 23 and 28 are each represented by 25.
Answer: 25
quiz.mistake: Uses a class limit, or the actual average of the values (23.5), instead of the class mark

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Grouping data into classes leads to some loss of information.
Reason (R): After grouping, individual values are replaced by the class mark.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Replacing actual values with the mid-point is exactly why detail is lost.
steps: A: grouping into classes causes some loss of information → true.
R: after grouping, individual values are replaced by the class mark → true.
Replacing actual values with the mid-point is exactly why detail is lost.
So R explains A → both true and R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Thinks grouped data keep every detail

quiz.q: Raw data: 5, 12, 18, 23, 7, 15, 28, 21, 9, 14. Using classes 0–10, 10–20, 20–30 (exclusive), what is the frequency of 10–20?
quiz.explain: Values from 10 up to but not including 20: 12, 18, 15, 14, so 4.
steps: Pick values ≥ 10 and < 20
Frequency = 4
Answer: 4
quiz.mistake: Includes values from another class or misses one

teach.ask: Gappu has 200 bird weights from 12 g to 96 g. 'How many classes should I make, and how wide?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Find the range, pick a width, divide to get the number of classes, then tally! Perfect table!
teach.nudge: Good! But how do you decide the number of classes? Which two numbers do you divide?

revise.summary: To build a frequency distribution, choose equal or unequal classes, find the number of classes, set clear limits, and count with tally marks. Grouping loses information because every value is treated as the class mark.
focus: Work out the number of classes from range and class width
Know when unequal classes are suitable
Count frequencies with tally marks
Explain loss of information in grouping and why open-ended classes are avoided
remember: Number of classes = range ÷ class width (round up to a whole number)
Tally marks: groups of five, four strokes with a fifth crossing them
After grouping, every value in a class is treated as equal to the class mark
traps: Don't round the number of classes down: round up
Don't count a tally group as one: each is five
Open-ended classes have no mid-point, so they are avoided where possible

learn.hook: A student scores exactly 20. Does she go in 10–20 or 20–30? The method you use decides, and getting it wrong double-counts students.
points: Exclusive method: the upper limit of one class is the lower limit of the next (10–20, 20–30). A value equal to the upper limit is excluded from that class and goes into the next. So 20 goes into 20–30.
Inclusive method: both limits are included in the class (10–19, 20–29). There is a gap between the upper limit of one class and the lower limit of the next.
Inclusive classes suit discrete data (like marks in whole numbers).

Adjustment: to make inclusive classes continuous, find the gap between one class's upper limit and the next class's lower limit, then subtract half the gap from every lower limit and add half to every upper limit. E.g. 10–19, 20–29 → 9.5–19.5, 19.5–29.5.
The class mark is unchanged by the adjustment, but the class width becomes the true width (10 instead of 9).

steps: Gap = 40 − 39 = 1, half gap = 0.5
Subtract 0.5 from lower limits: 29.5, 39.5, 49.5
Add 0.5 to upper limits: 39.5, 49.5, 59.5

learn.reallife: Census age tables use inclusive groups like 0–4, 5–9, 10–14 years, because age there is recorded in completed whole years.

items.text: Inclusive classes 20–29, 30–39: half the gap is ___.
In exclusive classes 10–20 and 20–30, the value 20 is placed in ___.

quiz.q: In the exclusive method with classes 40–50 and 50–60, a value of exactly 50 goes into:
quiz.explain: The upper limit is excluded, so 50 goes into the class starting at 50.
steps: Rule: in the exclusive method the upper limit of a class is not included in it.
So 40–50 holds values from 40 up to just below 50.
A value of exactly 50 is the lower limit of the next class.
So 50 goes into 50–60.
Answer: 50–60
quiz.mistake: Places the value in the class where it is the upper limit

quiz.q: In the inclusive method, classes are written as:
quiz.explain: Both limits are included, so classes do not share limits.
steps: Asked: how inclusive classes are written.
Rule: in the inclusive method both limits are included in the class.
So classes do not share limits: 10–19, 20–29, 30–39.
10–20, 20–30 shares limits, which is the exclusive method.
quiz.mistake: Confuses inclusive with exclusive form

quiz.q: Adjust the inclusive class 60–69 (next class 70–79). The adjusted class is:
steps: Gap = 1, half gap = 0.5
quiz.mistake: Adds the full gap or adjusts only one limit

quiz.q: For inclusive classes 10–14, 15–19, 20–24, what is the correction (half the gap) to be applied?
quiz.explain: Gap = 15 − 14 = 1, half of it is 0.5.
steps: Gap = next lower limit − this upper limit = 15 − 14 = 1
Half = 0.5
Answer: 0.5
quiz.mistake: Uses the full gap or the class width

quiz.q: After adjusting 10–14 to 9.5–14.5, what is the true class width?
quiz.explain: 14.5 − 9.5 = 5. The unadjusted '14 − 10 = 4' understates the width.
steps: Given adjusted class: 9.5–14.5.
Rule: width = upper limit − lower limit.
So the true class width is 5, not 14 − 10 = 4.
Answer: 5
quiz.mistake: Uses the unadjusted limits

quiz.q: The class mark of the inclusive class 20–29 is:
steps: Rule: class mark = (lower limit + upper limit)/2.
After adjustment to 19.5–29.5: (19.5 + 29.5)/2 = 49/2 = 24.5, unchanged.
So the class mark is 24.5.
Answer: 24.5
quiz.mistake: Assumes the mid-point is a round number like 25

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Inclusive classes need adjustment before drawing a histogram.
Reason (R): Inclusive classes have gaps between the upper limit of one class and the lower limit of the next.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: A histogram needs continuous classes, so the gaps must be removed by adjustment.
steps: A: inclusive classes need adjustment before drawing a histogram → true.
R: inclusive classes have gaps between one class's upper limit and the next lower limit → true.
A histogram needs continuous classes, so those gaps must be removed.
So R explains A → both true and R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Does not see why gaps matter

quiz.q: Marks (whole numbers) are to be grouped by the inclusive method with class width 10, starting at 0. The third class is:
quiz.explain: Classes are 0–9, 10–19, 20–29, so the third is 20–29.
steps: Inclusive classes of width 10 starting at 0 contain 10 whole numbers each.
1st class: 0–9; 2nd class: 10–19; 3rd class: 20–29.
20–30 and 21–30 would hold 11 or the wrong values; 30–39 is the 4th class.
So the third class is 20–29.
Answer: 20–29
quiz.mistake: Writes exclusive-style limits or starts the count at the wrong class

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'A bird weighs exactly 30 g. Should it go in 20–30 or 30–40? And what are classes like 20–29?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Exclusive: 30 goes to 30–40. Inclusive classes include both limits, and we adjust them by half the gap!
teach.nudge: Good! But how do we turn 20–29 and 30–39 into continuous classes? What do we add or subtract?

revise.summary: In exclusive classes the upper limit of one class is the lower limit of the next and is excluded from that class. In inclusive classes both limits are included; they are adjusted by subtracting and adding half the gap.
focus: Place a boundary value correctly in exclusive classes
Adjust inclusive classes to make them continuous
Find the correction, true class width and class mark
Explain why inclusive classes need adjustment before a histogram
remember: Exclusive: 10–20, 20–30; a value of 20 goes into 20–30
Adjustment: subtract half the gap from every lower limit, add half to every upper limit (10–19 → 9.5–19.5)
The class mark is unchanged by adjustment; the class width becomes the true width
traps: Don't place a value in the class where it is the upper limit (exclusive method)
Don't add the full gap or adjust only one limit
Don't assume the class mark is a round number: for 20–29 it is 24.5

learn.hook: Survey 30 families on how many members they have and the answers are just 2, 3, 4, 5, 6… Grouping them into classes like 2–4 would be silly. A frequency array is the neat solution.
points: A frequency array is a frequency distribution for a discrete variable: each value is listed with its frequency, without class intervals (e.g. household size 1, 2, 3… with number of households).
A univariate distribution deals with one variable. A bivariate (two-way) frequency distribution shows the joint frequencies of two variables in a table.
In a bivariate table, the rows are classes of one variable and the columns classes of the other; each cell shows how many units fall into both classes.
Example: companies classified by advertisement spending (rows) and sales (columns). Row and column totals give each variable's own (marginal) distribution.

example.q: A bivariate table shows firms by ad spend (₹ lakh) and sales (₹ lakh). The cell 'ad spend 10–20, sales 200–300' shows 4. What does it mean?
steps: Locate the row (ad spend 10–20) and column (sales 200–300).
The cell value counts firms that satisfy both conditions.
example.answer: 4 firms spend ₹10–20 lakh on ads and have sales of ₹200–300 lakh.

learn.reallife: A frequency array of household size from survey data helps planners decide what sizes of homes to build under housing schemes.

games.title: Match each to its distribution type
pairs: Household size with number of households
Sales and advertising spend in one table
Height and weight of students cross-classified

items.q: Same data. How many households in total?
Words: in, the, of, a. How many have 2 letters?

quiz.q: A frequency array is used for:
quiz.explain: A frequency array lists each value of a discrete variable with its frequency.
steps: Asked: what a frequency array is used for.
Rule: a frequency array lists each value of a discrete variable with its frequency.
Continuous variables need class intervals instead; two variables need a bivariate table.
So it is used for a discrete variable.
Answer: A discrete variable
quiz.mistake: Confuses frequency arrays with grouped continuous distributions

quiz.q: Household sizes from a survey: 3, 4, 2, 4, 5, 3, 4, 6, 4, 3. What is the frequency of household size 4?
quiz.explain: Size 4 appears four times.
steps: Positions with 4: 2nd, 4th, 7th, 9th
Frequency = 4
Answer: 4
quiz.mistake: Miscounts when scanning the list

quiz.q: Using the same data (3, 4, 2, 4, 5, 3, 4, 6, 4, 3), how many households have more than 4 members?
quiz.explain: More than 4 means 5 or 6: one each, so 2 households.
steps: Values > 4: 5 and 6
Count = 2
Answer: 2
quiz.mistake: Includes households of size 4

quiz.q: A distribution showing the joint frequencies of two variables is called:
quiz.explain: Bivariate means two variables classified together.
steps: Asked: the name for a distribution of joint frequencies of two variables.
'Bi' means two, so bivariate = two variables classified together.
Univariate and frequency arrays deal with one variable.
So the answer is 'Bivariate'.
Answer: Bivariate
quiz.mistake: Confuses bivariate with a cumulative table

quiz.q: In a bivariate table of 20 firms, the cell for 'ad spend 5–10' and 'sales 100–200' is 3, and the row total for 'ad spend 5–10' is 8. How many firms with ad spend 5–10 have sales outside 100–200?
quiz.explain: 8 − 3 = 5 firms in that row lie in other sales classes.
steps: Row total = 8
Answer: 5
quiz.mistake: Adds instead of subtracting from the row total

quiz.q: The row totals in a bivariate table give:
options: The distribution of the row variable alone
quiz.explain: Adding across a row gives that variable's own frequency for each class.
steps: Asked: what the row totals in a bivariate table give.
Each cell shows the joint frequency of a row class and a column class.
Adding across a row ignores the column variable.
So row totals give the distribution of the row variable alone.
Answer: The distribution of the row variable alone
quiz.mistake: Thinks totals still show the joint distribution

quiz.q: Count the letters in each word of the phrase 'DATA IS THE NEW OIL'. What is the frequency of 3-letter words?
quiz.explain: Word lengths: DATA 4, IS 2, THE 3, NEW 3, OIL 3. Three words have 3 letters.
steps: Lengths: 4, 2, 3, 3, 3
3-letter words: THE, NEW, OIL
Frequency = 3
Answer: 3
quiz.mistake: Miscounts letters or words

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): A bivariate distribution can show whether two variables tend to move together.
Reason (R): It records how often each combination of classes of the two variables occurs.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Seeing which combinations are common hints at how the variables are related.
steps: A: a bivariate distribution can show whether two variables move together → true.
R: it records how often each combination of classes occurs → true.
Seeing which combinations are common reveals how the variables are related.
So R explains A → both true and R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true and R explains A
quiz.mistake: Thinks a two-way table shows only one variable at a time

teach.ask: Gappu has data on both wing span and weight of 50 birds. 'Can I put both in one table? And how do I tabulate egg counts?'
teach.praise: Tweet! A bivariate table for two variables, cells show joint frequencies, and a frequency array for discrete egg counts!
teach.nudge: Good! What do we call a table showing two variables together? And what about a discrete variable like egg count?

revise.summary: A frequency array lists each value of a discrete variable with its frequency, without class intervals. A bivariate frequency distribution shows the joint frequencies of two variables in a two-way table.
focus: Build and read a frequency array
Read a cell of a bivariate table in words
Use row and column totals to find missing values and marginal distributions
remember: Frequency array: frequency distribution for a discrete variable
Bivariate (two-way) distribution: joint frequencies of two variables; row and column totals give each variable's own distribution
traps: Don't confuse a frequency array with a grouped continuous distribution
Row totals show the row variable alone, not the joint distribution
'More than 4' does not include 4
